Hunger Action Heroes · Email Program Proposal

An 8-email Klaviyo nurture for US school principals. Two months, awareness then conversion, with A/B subject lines throughout and every claim verified.

Prepared by Jacques Groenewald · JCE Media

Audience: US PrincipalsSender: Dana Williams Platform: Klaviyo flowStructure: Month A awareness, Month B conversion

🎯 Strategy at a glance

AudienceUS school principals and assistant principals, cold and nationwide. Risk-aware, mission-driven, and time-poor, so every line has to earn its place.
Goal and arcMonth A builds awareness and trust. Month B converts to a classroom kit, a sponsorship, or a founding spot on the schools leaderboard. One email per week.
AngleLead with the client's own framework (Cognitive Trust), real proof, and the in-development schools leaderboard as a founding-school hook. Warm and mission-led, never pushy, matched to how the client already writes.
Everything verifiedEvery claim is sourced from the client's own site and press coverage: 9,100 meals and 10,000 pounds of food rescued at Creekside, San Diego Business Journal's Most Innovative Campaign of 2025, a clinical-psychologist author, and heroes designed by students. Nothing invented.

⚙️ Klaviyo Flow Setup (so it builds exactly as briefed)

TriggerNew subscriber enters on tag (Batch 1 / Batch 2 / HAHU Contact), or manual add. Re-enrollment OFF to prevent duplicates.
CadenceOne email per week. Month A (Awareness) runs first for every new subscriber, then Month B (Conversion). Add a 7-day time delay between each.
Batch handlingBatch 1 (original list) skips any email they already received via a conditional split on a "received" tag, so no one gets a duplicate. New subscribers start clean at Month A, Email 1.
A/B subject testEach email has an A and a B subject line. In Klaviyo, turn on the message-level A/B test, 50/50 split, winner chosen by open rate after 4 hours, then auto-send the winner to the rest.
PersonalizationUses Klaviyo tags: {{ first_name|default:'there' }} and {{ school_name|default:'your school' }}. Map the sheet's "School Name" column to a school_name profile property on import.

Hi {{ first_name|default:'there' }},

Every year you are asked to grow empathy and character in your students, usually without extra hours to give your teachers. Most programs add to their plate. This one does not.

1 in 5 children in this country do not have access to enough food. Some of them are in {{ school_name|default:'your school' }}.

Hunger Action Heroes Unite! is a standards-aligned comic book and curriculum from a social enterprise of Feeding San Diego. It was written by a clinical psychologist (the creator of "Superhero Therapy") and illustrated by a professional comic artist, so it is engaging for students and credible for educators. Best of all, it runs with almost no teacher prep.

AWhy a comic works when a worksheet doesn't
BThese heroes were designed by kids, 14 and 17
Strategy / rationaleReal origin story (designed by kids, Comic-Con Museum, Iron Man costume designer) plus the real Cognitive Trust framing. Video links to the real origin page.

Health · Science · SEL · ELA · Project-Based Learning  |  A social enterprise of Feeding San Diego

Hi {{ first_name|default:'there' }},

Tell a student a statistic and it is gone by lunch. Give them a hero to root for, and it stays.

Here is the part students love: the two heroes, Demeter and Hunger Halter, were designed by kids. They came out of an art contest run by Feeding San Diego and the Comic-Con Museum, chosen from nearly 300 student submissions and brought to life by a costume designer who worked on the Iron Man and Captain America films.

In the story, journalist Julie Wilson becomes Demeter and joins Hunger Halter to rescue good food before it is wasted, so it reaches families who need it. We call the goal Cognitive Trust: making food support feel normal and values-based, never charity. When support is framed that way, students take part.

Hi {{ first_name|default:'there' }},

A new program is a risk. You do not want to hand teachers something unproven. So here is what real students did with it.

Two classes. Five months.
9,100 meals and 10,000 pounds of food rescued.

After reading the comic, students at Creekside Elementary organized a food drive, volunteered at Feeding San Diego, and fundraised for families facing hunger. The work was covered by the San Diego Union-Tribune and CBS 8, and the program was named the San Diego Business Journal's Most Innovative Awareness Campaign of 2025.

Before a principal says yes, the same handful of questions usually come up. Here they are, answered straight.

Is it standards-aligned? Yes. Health, Science, SEL, ELA, and project-based learning.

How much teacher prep? Very little. It is built to run out of the box.

Who made it? A clinical psychologist and a professional comic artist, for a social enterprise of Feeding San Diego.

Does it actually work? Two classes at Creekside rescued 10,000 pounds of food and provided 9,100 meals in five months.

What does it cost? From a single $6.99 comic to full classroom sets, with sponsorship available if budget is tight.

Hi {{ first_name|default:'there' }},

When this is a fit, the thing that usually stalls it is budget or timing. Three ways schools get started:

Start with one class. A single classroom or club is a low-cost first step.

Get it sponsored. A PTA, local business, or donor can fund a set. The gift-a-classroom option exists for exactly this.

Use existing SEL or character funds. It is standards-aligned, so it often fits a budget line you already have.

Worth knowing: every dollar spent provides two meals and prevents two pounds of food waste through Feeding San Diego, so the spend does double duty.

One honest note on timing: it lands best at the start of a unit or semester, so students complete the full project arc.

Month 3 - Recognition & Momentum

Wk 1 · The leaderboard is liveLaunch the interactive leaderboard to the founding schools collected in Month A. CTA: claim your spot.
